Cool. Now I just need to find out which genius decided to refuse using "ananas" like everyone else and go with the clearly more descriptive "pineapple".

You can blame Columbus for that! :-) He called them "piña de Indes" ("pine of the Indians") as they resembled a pine cone (sauce). I guess someone figured they should attach a known fruit to the name to make it clear what it was. Something similar was done in Italian for the tomato - the Italian word being "pomodoro" from "pomo d'oro" (literally: apple of gold / golden apple).

Apple was actually a word for any fruit.

One of the problems identifying apples in religion, mythology and folktales is that as late as the 17th century, the word "apple" was used as a generic term for all (foreign) fruit other than berries, but including nuts.

So pine-apple is pine-fruit, rather than anything specifically to do with apples.
Words that appear to share the same etymology, but in fact don't, are referred to as false cognates.
